results.title: The SAVRN Index: GPU Market Pricing in One Place
highlights:
The SAVRN Index is one place that captures all of the GPU market pricing and pricing changes. As of September 13, 2026, it tracks 732 prices from 54 providers 1. Specifically, every price is checked every three hours against the seller’s own feed or page. Moreover, every change is recorded with its date and its source 1. The same Index holds the register of 113 companies that fund, build, own and run AI infrastructure 1. In addition, it carries a scarcity index that reads 84.9 on a 0 to 100 scale, and the SAVRN Standard, the seven principles every offering is measured against 1. This post introduces each research topic in the Index. For each one, it says what the information is worth to a buyer, a seller, an investor or a planner.

...

In particular, those pages include the pricing pages of Anthropic,

...

A change read from a price page publishes once a second check sees the same new price 1. As a result, a page glitch never becomes a recorded move. Moreover, a move of more than 20 percent is held for a person to review before it publishes 1. Likewise, the same hold applies to a price that appears or disappears 1. Nothing is deleted. Specifically, a price that leaves a provider’s page is marked missing only after three consecutive checks fail to find it, and its history stays 1. Finally, where a page refuses automated checks, the Index says so on the row. It does not work around the refusal 1.

## What a GPU hour costs

The GPU page holds 190 prices from 26 providers across 10 GPUs 2. Specifically, every one is converted to one GPU for one hour and shown beside the provider’s own published price 2. However, GPUs are sold in whole units, so each card also shows the server or rack price. For example, an H100 server holds 8 GPUs, and a GB300 NVL72 rack holds 72 2.

The GPU page: every GPU's typical price by the hour, the whole-unit price, and how many prices sit behind it.

On September 13, 2026, the typical H100 price was $3.99 per GPU-hour, from 61 prices 2. That is $31.92 per hour for the 8-GPU server 2. Meanwhile, the H200 was $4.50, the B200 $6.97 and the B300 $7.89 2. In addition, the GB200 NVL72 was $10.58 per GPU-hour, or $761.90 per hour for the 72-GPU rack 2. Likewise, the GB300 NVL72 was $13.31, or $958.32 per rack-hour 2. Similarly, AMD’s MI300X was $3.45, the MI325X $2.90 and the MI355X $5.60 2. Notably, Vera Rubin NVL72 has no public price on any provider’s page 2.

### How wide one market is

In particular, the H100 shows the spread inside a single market. For instance, the cheapest H100 hour is $1.63 at Verda on spot 2. By contrast, the priciest on-demand hour is $12.29 at Microsoft Azure 2. Specifically, of the 61 H100 prices, 37 are on demand, 15 are reserved and 9 are spot 2. In addition, 4 offers carry no published price 2. Notably, nine of the 16 GB300 offers the Index tracks show no public price at all 2.

Every H100 price, cheapest first, with the seller's own published text beside the converted number.

...

The overview then reduces three businesses to one kilowatt-month. For example, a neocloud acting as developer charges $128 and keeps $24 4. Likewise, an AI cloud operator acting as tenant charges $1,358.70 and keeps $363 4. Meanwhile, a model company charges $2,717.85 and keeps $1,359 4. As a result, an investor can see in one chart where the margin sits at each layer of the same kilowatt.

...

The discounts are large and unstated. For instance, an Opus 5 input token lists at $5 per million and bills at $0.25 once it is cached and batched 4. Furthermore, five contracts withhold the tenant’s name, including CoreWeave’s build-to-suit and Riot’s investment-grade counterparty 4. In addition, TeraWulf redacted the capacity and rent for Lake Mariner, and Cipher and CleanSpark redacted their escalator percentages 4. Finally, full-stack contracts such as Nscale’s price the building and the compute together, with no separate rent 4.

## What moved

The changes page lists every price change the Index has recorded, newest first 4. Specifically, each row carries the old price, the new price, the percentage and the feed or page it came from 4. As of September 13, 2026 the Index had recorded 5 changes across its 732 tracked prices 4.

The changes record: every price move with the old price, the new price, the percentage and its source.

All five came on September 1, 2026, when Fireworks AI stepped up its on-demand GPU prices 4. For instance, GB300 went from $18 to $20 per GPU-hour, up 11.1 percent 4. Likewise, B300 went from $12 to $15, up 25 percent, and B200 from $10 to $13, up 30 percent 4. Similarly, H200 and H100 went from $7 to $8, up 14.3 percent each 4. This page is where the record of the market accumulates. Every future move appears here with its source, and the history is never deleted 4.

...

The companies page is the register: 113 companies that fund, build, own and run AI infrastructure, one page each 4. Specifically, each profile carries the company’s official logo and the social accounts the company links from its own site 4. In addition, the 39 that trade on NASDAQ or NYSE carry delayed live market data 4. Moreover, profiles draw on the Capital Atlas record of sites, financing transactions and deals 4. Likewise, where a company’s prices are tracked, its profile shows them 4.

Furthermore, the register groups the market into ten categories 4. Specifically, it holds six hyperscalers, three frontier AI labs, 23 neoclouds, 17 GPU clouds and two chipmakers 4. Similarly, it holds 21 data center developers, 19 private equity and infrastructure firms, 12 pension and state investment funds, and nine market intelligence and brokerage firms 4. Finally, it holds one controlled AI environment, which is SAVRN’s own row 4. For an investor or lender, the register is where a contract rate, a filing and a company’s record sit on one page.

...

What does an H100 cost per hour?

The typical H100 on-demand price on September 13, 2026 was $3.99 per GPU-hour, the median of 37 on-demand prices. However, the cheapest was $1.63 at Verda on spot, and the priciest on demand was $12.29 at Microsoft Azure 2.

results.title: The B200's rental price isn't the AI overcapacity tell
highlights:
- NVIDIA's B200 GPU hourly rental prices dropped 31% in June but surged 12% by September, contradicting "overbuilt" AI market fears.

- Price disparities (e.g., $3.70-$14.24/hour) reflect provider-specific factors, not silicon value, with no single "market price" for the chip.

- Key market signals show tight supply: 12-15 month GPU delivery delays, rising forward contract prices, and older chip rates increasing in 2026.

...

In late June, the hourly rental price of Nvidia's B200 GPU fell about 31% in three weeks, from a three-month high of $6.11 down to $4.22, and traders on the prediction-market platform Kalshi bet it would not get back to that high before the month was out. It was the cleanest possible version of the AI "overbuilt" fear: new capacity landing, prices collapsing, the cycle turning.

By early September the number had already turned around. The B200 spot price stood near $6.42 an hour, up about 12% over the month — and above the very peak that had triggered the panic. Older generations of the card were repricing up with it.

Here is the part the headline gets wrong. The B200 "rental price" is not the number that decides whether the AI buildout is overbuilt. It is the noisiest, most provider-dependent figure in the whole trade, and most of the time you are just watching your own index.

## Quick Backtesting Tool

## One chip, a dozen prices

The same physical GPU — a B200 with 192GB of HBM3e memory — rented for as little as $3.70 an hour on one neocloud in June and $14.24 an hour on a hyperscaler. That roughly 3.8x spread is not a difference in the silicon. It is provider margin, whether you are forced to buy an eight-GPU node instead of a single card, spot-versus-reserved billing, and the friction of a cloud service quota. The chip is identical in both listings.

There is no single "B200 price." Silicon Data publishes one index, Ornn another, SemiAnalysis a third, and every provider posts its own list price, and they do not agree. When a story or a title points at "the B200 rental price," it is pointing at one vendor's one index's one day's number and calling it the market.

That is a marketing-grade statistic, not an economic one.

...

The signal you cannot fake is the shape of the market, and on that shape the evidence points one way.

Forward contract prices are being renegotiated sharply upward, months ahead. Baseten, an AI inference provider, reported that its cloud vendors told it in May to expect its B200 rate to jump from $2.63 to $5.10 an hour at an October renewal — a 94% increase. The honest read, though, is that its baseline was a below-market rate it had locked in, and $5.10 is a catch-up to, and still slightly under, the prevailing spot. The magnitude is real, but it is "reprice to market," not "market prices double." The meaningful fact is directional: cloud providers are quoting increases months in advance, which tells you the buyer has no bargaining power.

The more durable number is delivery. Ordering roughly 1,000 GPUs now waits 12 to 15 months. That is the constraint no price index captures, because it is the supply side telling you it physically cannot meet demand on any shorter clock.

And the tell that overcapacity people keep missing: the old chips are getting more expensive, not cheaper. H100 and A100 rental rates are repricing up in 2026. If the market were flooded with surplus compute, you would be dumping last generation's hardware at a discount. Instead, new capacity is being absorbed and the installed base is holding — the pattern of demand that outruns supply, not demand that a chip shortage accidentally satisfies.

A spot price is a lagging, provider-specific snapshot. Forward contracts, delivery lead times, and the price of last generation's silicon are the leading, structural read — and all three say the compute market, as of September, is not overbuilt.

...

Two cautions keep this from being "prices are up, therefore buy." First, a high rental price is not the same as a high return for the people renting the cards out — a neocloud quoting $5.60 an hour still destroys equity if the machines sit idle or were financed expensively, so strong prices flatter Nvidia's demand more than they prove the neoclouds are safe. Second, the one thing that would actually change this read is supply arriving ahead of that demand: if the 12- to 15-month delivery clock starts to shrink and forward prices stop firming, the "not overbuilt" verdict flips, and the rental spot price is where you would see it first. Ironically, that makes the number the headline fixates on the right early warning — even though it is the wrong thesis.

results.title: Neoclouds vs. Hyperscalers: Who Will Win AI Cloud?
highlights:
But it is wrong to assume that hyperscalers cannot build specialized AI systems. AWS, for example, documents P5 instances with up to eight H100 GPUs, 3,200 Gbps Elastic Fabric Adapter networking, GPUDirect RDMA, and NVSwitch GPU peer-to-peer communication of up to 900 GB/s. AWS also offers H200 and Blackwell-based capacity.

...

### Potentially clearer pricing

A neocloud may present a simpler GPU-hour or reserved-capacity model. That does not automatically make it cheaper. Storage, egress, idle capacity, engineering effort, support, and minimum commitments can outweigh a lower accelerator rate.

...

## The economics: utilization matters more than the GPU-hour

The headline accelerator price is only one input. Buyers and investors should separate:

- On-demand pricing from reserved or committed capacity
- Advertised capacity from actually available capacity
- GPU utilization from nominal GPU ownership
- Training time to completion from hourly price
- Network and storage performance from accelerator specifications
- Infrastructure cost from financing expense
- Revenue backlog from realized revenue

A cheaper GPU-hour can produce a more expensive completed workload if the cluster is fragmented, jobs spend too long in a queue, distributed training scales poorly, checkpoint storage is slow, or failed jobs restart inefficiently. Data movement and egress can also materially change the result.

Hyperscalers are adapting their purchasing models. AWS Capacity Blocks for ML provide reservation-oriented access to scarce accelerator capacity. Its pricing page states that rates vary by accelerator, region, reservation timing, and supply and demand. As an observed snapshot, the page listed P5 H100 capacity at approximately $4.326 per accelerator-hour in several US regions and P6-B200 capacity at approximately $10.296 per accelerator-hour. Those figures were time-sensitive and should not be treated as permanent list prices.

results.title: AI Compute Financialization (II): Kalshi's Compute Forward Curve
highlights:
One is financing, turning future compute revenue into capital that can fund GPU purchases and data center buildout today. The other is commoditization, giving compute a spot price, a forward curve, and tools for hedging.

@Kalshi recently launched a compute forward curve derived from prediction market prices. It is trying to answer a simple question: what will one hour of B200 compute be worth a year from now? If the market can produce a credible answer, GPU residual value models, loan to value ratios, insurance, and hedging products can start to build on top of it.

What Kalshi launched is not actually a compute forward

In July 2026, Kalshi launched compute forward curves for Nvidia B200, H200, and A100 GPUs, calling them the first GPU compute forward curves derived from market prices.

At first glance, it looks like compute financialization jumped straight from having no price to having a forward curve. But the product has two separate layers.

The curve itself is not tradable. What people actually trade are dozens of binary contracts asking whether future GPU rental prices will be above a specific level. Kalshi combines those contract prices to estimate the market implied future rental price for each GPU.

So the more precise description is this: Kalshi did not create a traditional compute forward. It created a forward curve implied by prediction markets.

How it works

The settlement benchmark comes from Ornn. Ornn publishes a dollar denominated hourly rental price index for each GPU model. Kalshi then creates binary markets across models, price levels, and expiration dates.

For B200, one expiration date can have several contracts running at the same time:

- Will the hourly B200 price be above $3 on the settlement date?
- Will it be above $3.50?
- Will it be above $4?
- …until $7

Each YES contract trades between $0 and $1, which can be read as the market implied probability that the rental price will finish above that strike. Settlement is entirely in cash. If the Ornn index is above the threshold, YES pays $1. If not, it pays $0.

What does the curve look like today?

Now that the mechanism is clear, we can look at what the market is actually pricing. I pulled Kalshi’s monthly average markets through its public API on August 12, 2026. For each strike, I used the midpoint of the YES bid and ask as the probability that the price would finish above that level, then integrated across strikes to recover an implied hourly rental price.

From September 2026 to March 2027, the market expects B200 rental prices to fall by about 9%, then trade around $5.30 to $5.40. This is a backwardated curve. The market is basically saying B200 is expensive today and future supply should catch up.

The comparison across four GPU models is even more interesting. These are the implied prices from September 2026 to March 2027:

The newer the chip, the steeper the decline. Older chips have flatter curves, with a slight upward slope in some cases. B200 and H200 are still waiting for new capacity to come online, so the market expects prices to keep falling. H100 and A100 look closer to a floor, at least in the current market.

What does this mean for market participants?

- Neoclouds and AI data centers: The most direct use is setting the discount for long term contracts. If the B200 spot price is $5.83 today but the implied price six months out is only $5.30, a provider can use that forward price as a starting point when a customer commits demand in advance. It is not reliable enough to serve as a revenue forecast yet, but it could become a reference for pricing reserved capacity.
- Hedgers: Compute does not need to be perfectly standardized before hedging becomes useful. FX and commodity markets already use the most liquid benchmark for cross hedging. If B200 becomes the main benchmark, providers renting H200, B300, or GPUs in different regions could still use the B200 curve to hedge the overall direction of compute prices. Lenders financing GPUs could do the same, while accepting the remaining basis risk across models, providers, regions, and SLAs.

Most traders today are still speculators. That does not make the curve meaningless. Speculators often provide the first layer of price discovery and liquidity. The next real test is whether neoclouds, AI data centers, and lenders start using the benchmark to manage actual exposure.

The quality of the curve is still poor, though.

- Liquidity is concentrated in the near months. B200 open interest is 12,230 for September 2026, 1,103 for August 2027, and only 88 for September 2027. Further out, prices increasingly look like a market maker’s quote rather than a level backed by real trading.
- The strike range is fixed. Twelve of the thirteen B200 expirations only list nine strikes from $3 to $7, while the implied price sits around $5.30 to $5.90, already close to the upper bound. If the true price rises above $7, this integration method cannot capture it.
- Some quotes are simply inconsistent.

...

Suppose a neocloud is worried that B200 rental prices will fall below $5.50 in January 2027. It could buy NO contracts on ‘Will B200 be above $5.50?’ If the price does fall below that level, the NO contracts pay $1 and offset part of the rental revenue decline.

The payoff of a binary contract is fixed, though. Whether B200 falls to $5.40 or $3, one contract still pays only $1. To build something closer to the linear exposure of a traditional forward, a hedger would need to trade several strikes and combine a full strip of binary contracts.

Three problems remain:

- Basis risk: The Ornn index may not match the actual rental price for a specific company, region, provider, and SLA. That does not mean compute cannot support a forward market. It means the market first needs a common benchmark. Other exposures can use it as a proxy hedge and accept the remaining price difference.
- Liquidity: Each strike has its own order book, and trading activity and open interest are uneven.
- Tail risk: Kalshi only integrates across a limited strike range. The treatment of extreme prices outside that range directly affects the implied price.

results.title: Neoclouds: The Future of AI Workloads and Compute Power | The Innovation Dispatch
highlights:
Neoclouds are specialized cloud providers that focus on high-performance computing, particularly for artificial intelligence workloads. They distinguish themselves from traditional hyperscalers by offering highly specialized and significantly more cost-efficient GPU infrastructure tailored for demanding AI applications. For instance, a neocloud typically costs less than a hyperscaler for compute-intensive uses like AI, with one instance showing a 66% cost saving for certain GPUs, according to Coresite.

This cost advantage extends to specific hardware offerings. Lambda, a prominent neocloud provider, publishes the lowest B200 on-demand rate at $6.69 per GPU-hour, according to MarkTechPost. This ability to offer up to 66% cost savings on compute-intensive AI workloads indicates a shift in economic advantage for organizations prioritizing AI development.

Together AI added preemptible compute to GPU Clusters at a flat 50 percent of on-demand pricing. The option carries a five minute drain window and offers the same capacity for interruption tolerant jobs. It gives teams a lower cost path for training and batch inference.

results.title: The first GPUIndexes observation | GPUIndexes
highlights:
## The first observation

At 04:35 UTC on Sep 13, 2026, our first H100 SXM 80 GB snapshot contained 9 eligible single-GPU offer configurations from 6 providers. The provider-floor median was $3.08 per GPU-hour, with qualifying provider floors ranging from $2.79 to $4.29.

| Provider | Lowest eligible quote | Region |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lyceum | $2.7900 / GPU-hour | Europe |
| Massed Compute | $2.8900 / GPU-hour | us-central-12 |
| Ori | $2.9000 / GPU-hour | dallas-2 |
| VERDA | $3.2500 / GPU-hour | FIN-HEL |
| RunPod | $3.4900 / GPU-hour | global |
| Lambda Labs | $4.2900 / GPU-hour | us-south-3 |

## Why the basket matters

An H100 PCIe offer is not an H100 SXM offer. A price per GPU inside an eight-GPU instance does not mean that a single GPU can be rented at that price. The initial series fixes the model, memory, instance size and pricing lane before calculating a reference.

## A reference, not a transaction

The lowest provider quote is an observed floor. The median across providers describes the middle of those floors, with equal provider weight. It does not estimate the price of a typical completed transaction, the amount of supply, or every user’s total bill.
